title: Homeostasis
standard_text: Negative and positive feedback; thermoregulation; the endocrine system and hormones; the control of blood glucose; the nervous system, nerve impulses and synapses; and the kidney, water balance and excretion. (summary of The Ontario Curriculum, Grades 11 and 12: Science (2008), Biology, Grade 12, University Preparation (SBI4U), Strand E: Homeostasis)
meta_desc: Free Grade 12 Biology (SBI4U) worksheets on homeostasis: feedback loops, temperature control, hormones, blood glucose, nerve impulses, synapses and the kidney. 100 questions with answers.
key_big: Negative feedback brings a variable back to its set point.
key_sub: Hormones act slowly and widely; nerves act fast and locally.
body_html:
How to think about it

Homeostasis keeps the internal environment stable. In a negative feedback loop, a receptor detects a change, a control centre (often the hypothalamus) responds, and an effector reverses the change. Positive feedback (such as contractions during birth) increases the change until an end point.

Insulin lowers blood glucose and glucagon raises it. ADH makes the kidney collecting ducts reabsorb more water. A nerve impulse is an action potential: Na⁺ rushes in (depolarization), then K⁺ flows out (repolarization); at a synapse, neurotransmitters cross the gap.

Example

Blood glucose rises after a meal. Which hormone is released?

The pancreas responds to high glucose.

Answer: insulin

Example

A person is dehydrated. What happens to ADH and urine?

More ADH, more water reabsorbed

Answer: ADH rises and urine is more concentrated

Common mistakes

  • Saying insulin turns glucose into energy: it makes cells take up glucose and store it as glycogen.
  • Calling a fever a positive feedback loop.
  • Thinking impulses jump across a synapse electrically.

faq.q: What is the role of the hypothalamus?
faq.a: It is the control centre for temperature and water balance, and it links the nervous and endocrine systems.
It filters blood, reabsorbs useful substances and water, and makes urine.

items.q: An impulse travels 40 mm along an axon in 4.0 ms. Calculate its speed in m s⁻¹.
How does it help body temperature control when shivering starts?
c: Less blood flows near the skin surface, so less heat is lost.
Less heat is lost by evaporation.
Rapid muscle contractions release heat from respiration.
More blood flows near the skin surface, so more heat is lost by radiation.
items.e: The hypothalamus detects blood temperature and controls these responses.

items.q: Drinking water when you are thirsty is an example of which kind of feedback?
c: positive feedback (it makes the change bigger)
items.e: Negative feedback keeps conditions stable.

items.q: Stomata closing when a plant is short of water is an example of which kind of feedback?
c: positive feedback (it makes the change bigger)
items.e: Negative feedback keeps conditions stable.

items.q: Insulin released after a meal is an example of which kind of feedback?
c: positive feedback (it makes the change bigger)
items.e: Negative feedback keeps conditions stable.

items.q: An impulse travels 30 mm along an axon in 5.0 ms. Calculate its speed in m s⁻¹.
Benjamin's body temperature is 38.8 °C. The body sweats. Why?
c: to lose heat and cool down
to make heat and warm up
items.e: The response opposes the change.

items.q: When sweating increases, which is the body responding to?
items.e: Water in sweat evaporates, taking heat (latent heat) from the skin.

items.q: Which hormone raises blood glucose?
items.e: It is made by α cells.

items.q: How does it help body temperature control when arterioles in the skin constrict (vasoconstriction)?
c: Less heat is lost by evaporation.
Less blood flows near the skin surface, so less heat is lost.
Rapid muscle contractions release heat from respiration.
items.e: The hypothalamus detects blood temperature and controls these responses.

items.q: Emma's body temperature is 37.8 °C (normal is about 37 °C). What does the body do?
c: sweating and blood vessels in the skin widen
shivering and blood vessels in the skin narrow
items.e: Negative feedback moves it back toward 37 °C.

items.q: Nathan's body temperature is 36.4 °C. The body shivers. Why?
c: to make heat and warm up
to lose heat and cool down
items.e: The response opposes the change.

items.q: Platelets calling more platelets to a cut until it clots is an example of which kind of feedback?
c: positive feedback (it makes the change bigger)
items.e: Negative feedback keeps conditions stable.

items.q: How does it help body temperature control when the metabolic rate increases?
c: Water in sweat evaporates, taking heat (latent heat) from the skin.
Rapid muscle contractions release heat from respiration.
More blood flows near the skin surface, so more heat is lost by radiation.
items.e: The hypothalamus detects blood temperature and controls these responses.

items.q: Glucagon released when blood sugar is low is an example of which kind of feedback?
c: positive feedback (it makes the change bigger)
items.e: Negative feedback keeps conditions stable.

items.q: When shivering starts, which is the body responding to?
items.e: Rapid muscle contractions release heat from respiration.

items.q: The refractory period of a neurone is 1.5 ms. Calculate the maximum frequency of impulses, in impulses per second.
items.e: Maximum frequency = 1 ÷ 0.00150 s = 667 Hz.

items.q: When the metabolic rate increases, which is the body responding to?
items.e: More respiration releases more heat.

items.q: Sweating when you are hot is an example of which kind of feedback?
c: positive feedback (it makes the change bigger)
items.e: Negative feedback keeps conditions stable.

items.q: The kidneys filter 125 mL of blood plasma per minute and produce 1.0 mL of urine per minute. What percentage of the filtrate is reabsorbed?
What is the hormone made by the pineal gland?
items.e: It controls the sleep–wake cycle.

items.q: Which hormone is responsible for development of T-lymphocytes?
items.e: Thymosins: development of T-lymphocytes.

items.q: Which hormone is responsible for the emergency (fight or flight) response?
items.e: Adrenaline: the emergency (fight or flight) response.

items.q: What is the main role of cortisol?
c: raising blood glucose and reducing inflammation
raising the Ca²⁺ level in the blood
items.e: Cortisol: raising blood glucose and reducing inflammation.

items.q: What is the main role of thymosins?
c: raising the Ca²⁺ level in the blood
items.e: Thymosins: development of T-lymphocytes.

items.q: Which hormone acts on the exocrine pancreas to release water and bicarbonate ions?
items.e: It is made in the duodenum.

items.q: What is the main role of melatonin?
c: the daily (24-hour) rhythm of sleep and wakefulness
items.e: Melatonin: the daily (24-hour) rhythm of sleep and wakefulness.

items.q: Which gland secretes oxytocin?
c: the Leydig cells of the testis
the posterior pituitary (made in the hypothalamus)
items.e: Oxytocin is made in the posterior pituitary (made in the hypothalamus).

items.q: Which hormones are made in the hypothalamus but stored in the posterior pituitary?
items.e: They travel down nerve axons.

items.q: Which hormone is responsible for raising blood glucose?
items.e: Glucagon: raising blood glucose.

items.q: Which gland secretes thymosins?
c: the posterior pituitary (made in the hypothalamus)
items.e: Thymosins is made in the thymus.

items.q: What is the main role of testosterone?
items.e: Testosterone: male secondary sexual characters.

items.q: Which gland secretes growth hormone?
c: the posterior pituitary (made in the hypothalamus)
items.e: Growth hormone is made in the anterior pituitary.

items.q: Which gland secretes ANF?
c: the Leydig cells of the testis
the atrial wall of the heart
items.e: ANF is made in the atrial wall of the heart.

items.q: Which gland secretes testosterone?
c: the Leydig cells of the testis
items.e: Testosterone is made in the Leydig cells of the testis.

items.q: Which gland secretes melatonin?
c: the atrial wall of the heart
items.e: Melatonin is made in the pineal gland.

items.q: Which hormone is responsible for controlling the basal metabolic rate?
items.e: Thyroxine: controlling the basal metabolic rate.

items.q: What is the role of glucocorticoids such as cortisol?
c: raising blood glucose (gluconeogenesis) and suppressing inflammation
items.e: They are made in the adrenal cortex.

items.q: What is the main role of progesterone?
c: the daily (24-hour) rhythm of sleep and wakefulness
lowering the Ca²⁺ level in the blood
items.e: Progesterone: maintaining pregnancy.

items.q: Which hormone is called the hormone of pregnancy?
items.e: It keeps the uterus lining ready.

items.q: What is the role of the liver in controlling blood glucose?
c: it filters glucose out of urine
it converts glucose to glycogen and back again
items.e: Liver cells have insulin and glucagon receptors.

items.q: After a meal, blood glucose rises from 4.8 to 10 mmol/L in 60 minutes. Calculate the mean rate of increase.
How does IAA cause positive phototropism in shoots?
c: it moves to the lit side, which grows faster
it stops growth on the shaded side
it moves to the shaded side, which grows faster
it is destroyed on the shaded side
items.e: The shoot bends towards light.

items.q: Arjun's blood glucose is 3.8 mmol/L. After the pancreas responds, what happens to the blood glucose level?
c: It keeps moving further from normal.
items.e: Negative feedback.

items.q: After a meal, blood glucose rises from 5.2 to 6.8 mmol/L in 90 minutes. Calculate the mean rate of increase.
The kidneys filter 130 mL of blood plasma per minute and produce 1.2 mL of urine per minute. What percentage of the filtrate is reabsorbed?
Which part of the kidney is affected by ADH?
items.e: Aquaporins are inserted into the membranes.

items.q: Benjamin's blood glucose is 3.2 mmol/L (normal is about 4–7 mmol/L). Which hormone does the pancreas release more of?
items.e: High glucose → insulin; low glucose → glucagon.

items.q: Priya's blood glucose is 9.0 mmol/L (normal is about 4–7 mmol/L). What does the liver do?
c: Glucose is converted to glycogen and stored.
Glycogen is converted to glucose, which is released into the blood.
items.e: Insulin and glucagon both act on the liver.

items.q: Olivia's blood glucose is 9.5 mmol/L (normal is about 4–7 mmol/L). Which hormone does the pancreas release more of?
items.e: High glucose → insulin; low glucose → glucagon.

items.q: Which hormone lowers blood glucose?
items.e: It is made by β cells in the islets of Langerhans.

items.q: Where does ultrafiltration happen in the kidney?
items.e: High blood pressure forces small molecules out.

items.q: An impulse travels 60 mm along an axon in 0.80 ms. Calculate its speed in m s⁻¹.
After a meal, blood glucose rises from 5.0 to 8.5 mmol/L in 90 minutes. Calculate the mean rate of increase.
What is homeostasis?
c: keeping the internal environment within restricted limits
changing body temperature with the weather
items.e: For example core temperature, blood glucose and water potential.

items.q: Aiden's blood glucose is 3.4 mmol/L (normal is about 4–7 mmol/L). What does the liver do?
c: Glucose is converted to glycogen and stored.
Glycogen is converted to glucose, which is released into the blood.
items.e: Insulin and glucagon both act on the liver.

items.q: What is the main cause of type 2 diabetes?
c: too little glucose in the diet
body cells no longer respond properly to insulin
the pancreas makes no insulin at all
items.e: Linked to obesity; controlled by diet and exercise.

items.q: An impulse travels 120 mm along an axon in 0.80 ms. Calculate its speed in m s⁻¹.
After a meal, blood glucose rises from 4.5 to 9.0 mmol/L in 60 minutes. Calculate the mean rate of increase.
How does insulin lower blood glucose?
c: it is broken down into glucose
it increases glucose uptake by cells and activates glycogenesis
it makes the kidneys excrete glucose
items.e: More glucose channel proteins appear in membranes.

items.q: Which ions rush into an axon during depolarization?
items.e: The inside becomes positive.

items.q: Which type of muscle fibre is adapted for endurance?
c: slow-twitch fibres with many mitochondria and myoglobin
items.e: They respire aerobically.

items.q: What is a reflex arc?
c: a pathway from receptor to sensory, relay and motor neurone to an effector
a synapse in the brain only
items.e: Reflexes are rapid and protective.

items.q: What is the all-or-nothing principle?
c: a stimulus above the threshold always gives a full-size action potential
bigger stimuli give bigger action potentials
every stimulus gives an action potential
action potentials fade along the axon
items.e: Stronger stimuli give more frequent impulses.

items.q: The refractory period of a neurone is 0.80 ms. Calculate the maximum frequency of impulses, in impulses per second.
items.e: Maximum frequency = 1 ÷ 8.00 × 10−4 s = 1250 Hz.

items.q: Why are synapses unidirectional?
c: the synaptic cleft is too wide
neurotransmitter is released only from the presynaptic side and receptors are only on the postsynaptic side
the axon only conducts one way
items.e: So impulses travel one way.

items.q: What triggers the release of neurotransmitter at a synapse?
c: Ca²⁺ ions entering the presynaptic knob
items.e: Vesicles fuse with the membrane.

items.q: What causes depolarization in an action potential?
c: K⁺ channels open and K⁺ leaves
voltage-gated Na⁺ channels open and Na⁺ ions diffuse in
items.e: The inside becomes positive.

items.q: What is a generator potential?
c: a depolarization of a receptor membrane caused by a stimulus
items.e: If it reaches threshold, an action potential follows.

items.q: What causes repolarization?
c: Na⁺ channels close and voltage-gated K⁺ channels open, so K⁺ diffuses out
items.e: The potential falls back towards rest.

items.q: Where is the cardiovascular control centre?
items.e: It changes heart rate through the SAN.

items.q: An impulse travels 120 mm along an axon in 5.0 ms. Calculate its speed in m s⁻¹.
An impulse travels 40 mm along an axon in 0.80 ms. Calculate its speed in m s⁻¹.
The refractory period of a neurone is 1.2 ms. Calculate the maximum frequency of impulses, in impulses per second.
items.e: Maximum frequency = 1 ÷ 0.00120 s = 833 Hz.

items.q: Which cells form the myelin sheath in the peripheral nervous system?
items.e: Gaps between them are nodes of Ranvier.

items.q: An impulse travels 10 mm along an axon in 1.2 ms. Calculate its speed in m s⁻¹.
The refractory period of a neurone is 10 ms. Calculate the maximum frequency of impulses, in impulses per second.
items.e: Maximum frequency = 1 ÷ 0.0100 s = 100 Hz.

items.q: An impulse travels 40 mm along an axon in 5.0 ms. Calculate its speed in m s⁻¹.
What is summation at a synapse?
c: several small stimuli add together to reach the threshold
items.e: Spatial or temporal summation.

items.q: The refractory period of a neurone is 2.5 ms. Calculate the maximum frequency of impulses, in impulses per second.
items.e: Maximum frequency = 1 ÷ 0.00250 s = 400 Hz.

items.q: Is glucose normally found in the urine of a healthy person?
items.e: All glucose is reabsorbed in the proximal tubule.

items.q: You drink several glasses of a dilute fruit drink. What kind of urine is produced?
c: a large volume of dilute urine
a small volume of concentrated urine
items.e: More ADH → more water reabsorbed → less, more concentrated urine.

items.q: Besides the kidneys, which organ removes CO₂?
items.e: Skin also removes some salts in sweat.

items.q: What is glycogenolysis?
items.e: Stimulated by glucagon and adrenaline.

items.q: You wake up after a night of not drinking anything. What kind of urine is produced?
c: a small volume of concentrated urine
a large volume of dilute urine
items.e: More ADH → more water reabsorbed → less, more concentrated urine.

items.q: What is the second messenger in the action of adrenaline and glucagon?
items.e: It activates protein kinase.

items.q: How much urine does a healthy adult pass each day?
items.e: Over 99% of the filtrate is reabsorbed.

items.q: The kidneys filter 110 mL of blood plasma per minute and produce 0.80 mL of urine per minute. What percentage of the filtrate is reabsorbed?
What is the glomerulus?
c: the part that keeps the medulla salty so concentrated urine can form
the part that reabsorbs nearly all glucose, amino acids and 70–80% of salts and water
the tuft of capillaries where ultrafiltration happens
the cup-shaped part of the nephron around the glomerulus
items.e: Glomerulus: the tuft of capillaries where ultrafiltration happens.

items.q: What is the Bowman's capsule?
c: the hormone that increases Na⁺ reabsorption in the DCT
the cup-shaped part of the nephron around the glomerulus
the factor from the heart that widens blood vessels and lowers blood pressure
the cells that release renin when blood pressure falls
items.e: Bowman's capsule: the cup-shaped part of the nephron around the glomerulus.

items.q: The kidneys filter 120 mL of blood plasma per minute and produce 2.0 mL of urine per minute. What percentage of the filtrate is reabsorbed?
Which term matches this description: the part where conditional reabsorption of Na⁺ and water takes place?
items.e: Distal convoluted tubule (DCT): the part where conditional reabsorption of Na⁺ and water takes place.

items.q: What is the ADH (vasopressin)?
c: the cup-shaped part of the nephron around the glomerulus
the factor from the heart that widens blood vessels and lowers blood pressure
the part that reabsorbs nearly all glucose, amino acids and 70–80% of salts and water
the hormone that increases water reabsorption
items.e: ADH (vasopressin): the hormone that increases water reabsorption.

items.q: The kidneys filter 130 mL of blood plasma per minute and produce 0.50 mL of urine per minute. What percentage of the filtrate is reabsorbed?
Why does glucose appear in the urine of someone with untreated diabetes?
c: the carrier proteins in the proximal tubule cannot reabsorb all of it
items.e: Blood glucose is too high.

items.q: Is mineral salts found in the glomerular filtrate of a healthy person?
items.e: It is small enough to be filtered through the glomerulus.

items.q: You eat very salty food. What kind of urine is produced?
c: a large volume of dilute urine
a small volume of concentrated urine
items.e: More ADH → more water reabsorbed → less, more concentrated urine.

items.q: Which term matches this description: the cup-shaped part of the nephron around the glomerulus?
items.e: Bowman's capsule: the cup-shaped part of the nephron around the glomerulus.

items.q: Which term matches this description: the part that keeps the medulla salty so concentrated urine can form?
items.e: Loop of Henle: the part that keeps the medulla salty so concentrated urine can form.

items.q: Is amino acids found in the glomerular filtrate of a healthy person?
items.e: It is small enough to be filtered through the glomerulus.
